Appendix A Related Work We review label biases and demonstration order in ICL, mechanistic accounts, and diffusion language models, closing with the interpretability tools adopted in our analysis. Label Biases and Demonstration Order in ICL. Lu et al. [ 3 ] showed that permuting the same demonstrations can swing ICL accuracy from near-random to near-optimal, establishing order sensitivity as a central concern. Min et al. [ 18 ] found that randomly replacing demonstration labels barely hurts performance: demonstrations primarily convey the label space, the input distribution, and the response format. Our results expose the flip side: while the truth of demonstration labels may be optional, which words occupy the label space is consequential; switching the label pair from positive/negative to circle/square induces query-independent collapse across all five architectures. Zhao et al. [ 4 ] identified majority label bias, recency bias, and common token bias [ 7 ] and proposed contextual calibration; later work measured robustness to the majority-label bias induced by skewed demonstration distributions, finding robustness boundaries that vary widely across models and tasks [ 19 ] , and defined a typology of vanilla, context, and domain label biases [ 20 ] . All of these methods correct the label log-odds (the quantity we measure as separation) against a chosen reference point; Zhou et al. [ 8 ] unify the family as subtracting a context bias and show that a batch-mean reference dominates. Our use is orthogonal: rather than correcting predictions, we read the joint distribution of the shared bias and the query-dependent component, which turns the family itself into a probe of where the bias lives (Appendix E ). The domain-label bias of Fei et al. [ 20 ] (task accuracy pinned at chance by the label words themselves) anticipates the label-word sensitivity we isolate; we extend it to strictly class-balanced arrangements, across architectures, and with the bias decomposed at the output head. Our collapse arises under strictly class-balanced arrangements, placing it outside the majority-label-bias setting; label words have been varied only jointly with wholesale template changes [ 4 ] , not isolated under a fixed template, and, to our knowledge, collapse has not been characterized as a query-independent failure across architectures. This is the gap our paper addresses. Induction Heads and ICL Mechanisms. Induction heads [ 21 ] are a hypothesized mechanism for much of in-context learning, raising the question of whether label collapse is simply an induction failure. The evidence in Section 4 argues that it is not: collapse is label-word-specific rather than pattern-specific, its direction is arrangement-invariant for strong-bias pairs, and demonstration and query information remain decodable even when the model is collapsed. Induction heads explain how models copy patterns, but not which label token dominates when the copied signal and the output projection disagree; our separation diagnostic measures exactly this disagreement. Complementing this mechanistic line, task-vector analyses locate the demonstration-induced adaptation in low-dimensional representation shifts [ 22 ] , and geometric studies contrast prompt-induced adaptation with the mechanism that transforms base representations during instruction tuning [ 23 ] ; both operate at the representation level, whereas our diagnostic reads the label decision directly at the output projection. Diffusion Language Models and ICL. Discrete diffusion LMs generate text by iteratively denoising a masked sequence rather than decoding left to right [ 24 ] : MDLM [ 25 ] showed that simple masked diffusion with a simplified objective is more performant than previously thought, LLaDA [ 5 ] scaled it to 8B parameters, Dream [ 26 ] demonstrated competitive reasoning and planning, and iLLaDA [ 9 ] was trained from scratch with fully bidirectional attention (12T tokens), releasing Base and SFT variants. SFT is known to degrade pre-trained capabilities in AR models [ 17 ] ; we extend this observation to dLLMs, where it can alter label bias directions between Base and Instruct variants. Contemporaneous work has begun to characterize dLLM in-context behavior: Piskorz et al. show that mask tokens are not passive placeholders (where relevant demonstrations sit relative to them shapes what the model comprehends) and that performance varies with how the same in-context examples are ordered [ 6 ] . Within this emerging literature our contribution is specific: we isolate query-independent label failure as a phenomenon, characterize it across AR and dLLM families under matched protocols, and show that dLLMs share the AR label-collapse phenotype while raising new questions about how iterative denoising interacts with label biases. Probing and Logit Lens. Linear probing [ 27 ] trains classifiers on hidden states to test what information is encoded; the logit lens [ 15 ] decodes intermediate layers through the output vocabulary. We apply the logit lens to dLLMs, reading label-token logits at the masked answer position across all transformer layers (Section 4 ), to locate where the label bias is set; extending trained probes and denoising-step trajectories to dLLMs remains open. Appendix D Parsing Protocol and Artifact Audit Generation outputs are read at the text level: the first content token of the output (skipping leading newlines and whitespace) is matched, case-insensitively, against the two label words of the pair; pos_rate is the fraction of the 200 queries whose output matches the positive label, and outputs matching neither word count as invalid. Three artifact classes initially confounded this reading, and Table 1 flags any cell where more than 30% of outputs remain invalid even after correction ( † ): (i) Tokenizer splits. A label word may tokenize into multiple pieces, so first-token matching fails: “ancient” splits in all three dLLM vocabularies (“an”+“cient”), “toxic” in Qwen3.5 (“to”+“xic”), and “clean”, “kind”, “cruel”, “quiet”, “rich”, and “wet” split in various models.
